papers.title: Tight Analysis for Online Generalized Network Design with Power Functions
papers.abstract: We study the online generalized network design problem with heterogeneous power costs. Here, a sequence of $N$ requests arrive online, each of which needs to be assigned to some subset of available resources $E$. Each resource $e\in E$ has its own coefficient $ξ_e>0$ and exponent $p_e\ge 1$, where the cost of a load vector $L\in \mathbb{R}^E_+$ is $Φ(L)=\sum_{e\in E}ξ_e L_e^{p_e}$. We provide a simple analysis for the natural greedy algorithm that $τ$-approximately minimizes the increase in $Φ$ for each online request. Our competitive ratio is at most $(\frac{p}{\ln 2})^p$ when $τ=1$ and is roughly $(τp)^p$ as $τ$ grows large; here $p=\max_{e\in E} p_e$. This improves over a prior competitive ratio of $2(eτp)^p$ that relied on a modified greedy algorithm and a more complex analysis. Moreover, our bound (with $τ=1$) is asymptotically optimal: it matches the $(1.443p)^p$ lower bound for deterministic online algorithms. We also provide a nuanced exponent-dependent bound that, combined with prior results, provides an improved competitive ratio for (dis)economies of scale cost functions; here, the cost of resource $e$ has the form $σ_e + ξ_e\cdot x^{p_e}$ if $x>0$ (and zero if $x=0$). These results apply to several fundamental network problems such as multicommodity routing (where $τ=1$), Steiner tree connectivity (where $τ=1.39$) and directed Steiner connectivity (where $τ$ is poly-logarithmic).

papers.title: Trusted Advice for Scheduling on Unrelated Machines
papers.abstract: Scheduling on unrelated parallel machines under standard objectives, such as makespan minimization or max-min fairness, has posed fundamental theoretical challenges for decades. A prominent example is the longstanding factor 2 approximation barrier for the Min Makespan problem established by Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990). We investigate these fundamental challenges within the framework of algorithms with trusted advice. We consider a setting in which a trusted oracle is accessed once and reveals partial but entirely accurate structural information about an optimal solution. This framework allows us to quantify the improvements in approximation guarantees enabled by various trusted advice. We formalize a hierarchy of trusted advice oracles, ranging from a strong oracle that reveals the exact assignments of long jobs to a weaker oracle that indicates only which machines process such jobs. By exploiting this information, we obtain approximation guarantees beyond the classical worst-case barriers. In particular, we show that even the weakest oracle improves the approximation ratio for Min Makespan to $\sqrt{3}\approx 1.732$. We also obtain improved ratios of $(\sqrt{33}+1)/4\approx 1.686$ and $(5\sqrt{7})/8 \approx 1.654$ for Restricted Assignment and Graph Balancing, respectively. For the max-min fairness objective, known as the Santa Claus problem, we obtain a 2-approximation using our weak oracle. Finally, we show that these problems remain NP-hard to approximate within certain constant factors even with the trusted advice oracles considered. Interestingly, for the Santa Claus problem, we show a lower bound of 2 which is tight and matches the classical oracle-free bound.

papers.title: Optimal XOR Lemmas for Information Complexity
papers.abstract: Information complexity studies how much information the parties to a communication protocol must reveal to each other about their inputs to accomplish a given task. For a Boolean-valued communication problem $F$, let ${\rm IC}_ε(F)$ denote its information complexity with error $ε$, and let $F^{\oplus n}$ denote the XOR of $n$ independent instances of $F$. A fundamental question is whether information complexity obeys an XOR lemma, ${\rm IC}_{1/3}(F^{\oplus n})=Ω(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{1/(3n)}(F))$, which would match the trivial upper bound. Previous work either established the $n$-fold increase in information cost without the $n$-fold decrease in error (Bar-Yossef et al., FOCS 2002) or proved a lower bound with a subtracted penalty proportional to the input length of $F$ (Sawettamalya and Yu, STOC 2025). In particular, the question has remained open even for the XOR of $n$ or fewer copies of a function $F:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$. We completely resolve the question of XOR lemmas for information complexity, for every error $0\leε\le1/3$. For total functions $F$, we prove that ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=Θ(n\cdot{\rm IC}_{ε/n}(F))$ unless $F$ has the degenerate form $F(x,y)=a(x)\oplus b(y)$, in which case ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=O(1)$. For the richer class of partial functions, we obtain the characterization ${\rm IC}_ε(F^{\oplus n})=Θ({\rm IC}_ε(F)+n\cdot{\rm SIC}_{ε/n}(F))$, where ${\rm SIC}$ is the information complexity of protocols in which Alice and Bob privately output bits whose XOR is the answer. Finally, we prove an optimal distributional XOR lemma, for every function $F$ and every distribution. We obtain an optimal direct sum theorem to accompany each of our XOR lemmas. All implicit constants are absolute. Our work contributes a novel combination of information-theoretic and geometric techniques.

papers.title: Via a New LP Relaxation: Stronger Performance Guarantees for WSEPT, and an LP-Based Proof of Kawaguchi & Kyan
papers.abstract: We present a new linear programming relaxation for minimizing the total weighted completion time on identical parallel machines. Its right-hand side is supermodular, so the relaxation can be solved by a greedy algorithm. We show that the WSPT rule is within a factor $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{2})$ of the optimal LP value. This bounds the integrality gap of the relaxation and gives a short, LP-based proof of the tight bound of Kawaguchi and Kyan on the performance of WSPT. We then turn to the stochastic version of the problem, in which processing times are independent random variables whose squared coefficients of variation are at most~$Δ$. A variance-corrected version of the new LP relaxation is valid for all non-anticipatory policies, and we show that WSEPT is within a factor $1 + (1 + Δ)/(3 + \sqrt{7 + 2 Δ})$ of it for $Δ\ge 1$, for any number of machines. This is $O(\sqrtΔ)$, whereas all previous guarantees for this problem grow linearly in $Δ$. Up to a constant factor, our bound matches the known $Ω(\sqrtΔ)$ lower bound for WSEPT. For $Δ\le 1$, we recover the best known bounds.

papers.title: Weighted Flow Time Does Not Admit Constant-Competitive Randomized Algorithms
papers.abstract: We study online preemptive scheduling on a single machine with the objective of minimizing the total weighted flow time. Bansal and Chan (SODA 2009) showed that no deterministic online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive for this problem. We show that no randomized online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary either. This settles the remaining case of the long-standing question whether the problem admits an $O(1)$-competitive online algorithm. Quantitatively, every randomized online algorithm has a competitive ratio in $Ω(\min\{\log\log W,\log\log\log\min\{P,D,n\}\})$, where $n$ is the number of jobs and $W$, $P$, and $D$ are the ratios of the largest to the smallest job weight, size, and density (weight divided by size), respectively. The lower bound also holds with high probability, with the same asymptotic dependence on the instance parameters. For every $ρ\ge1$ and every randomized online algorithm, there is an instance on which the cost of the algorithm is at least $ρ$ times the optimal cost with probability at least $1-2^{-2^ρ}$. Both lower bounds hold even if the algorithm knows in advance the size and weight of every job in release order and, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every interarrival time up to a factor of $1+\varepsilon$.

papers.title: Unshardable Codes
papers.abstract: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.

papers.title: Constrained Online Selection with Predictions: Matroid Secretary, Knapsack, and Matching
papers.abstract: We study learning-augmented algorithms for constrained online selection problems, including the secretary problem under matroid and knapsack constraints, and the edge-weighted online bipartite matching problem with random vertex arrivals. In each, items arrive in a uniformly random order, and their values are revealed only on arrival. The goal is to select a set of items with nearly maximum total value, subject to the constraints (matroid, knapsack, or matching). In the learning-augmented setting, item value predictions are given in advance. We seek algorithms that are both consistent, in that accurate predictions lead to near-optimal selection, and robust, in that they obtain strong worst-case bounds even when predictions are inaccurate. Building on work of Fujii and Yoshida (2024) on the learning-augmented secretary problem, we study a method that follows the predicted optimum until an item with a large enough prediction error is observed. At that point, it reverts to running a worst-case competitive algorithm. We make a simple but critical modification: the first item with a large prediction error is selected with a carefully chosen probability. With this modification, we prove a general result, showing that if the underlying worst-case algorithm is $α$-competitive for $α\in(0,1]$, this approach achieves competitive ratio $\max\{\fracα{2(1+α)},\frac{1-ε}{1+ε}\}$, where $ε$ is the maximum relative error of any prediction. That is, the algorithm is perfectly consistent, achieving competitive ratio $1$ as $ε\to 0$, and robust up to a constant factor relative to the worst-case baseline. For all three problems we study, $α= 1/e$, and our result is the first to achieve consistency and constant-factor robustness. We hope that our general analysis framework can be applied to other learning-augmented online decision-making problems.

papers.title: A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

papers.title: Trajectory Visibility at First Sight
papers.abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, and let two moving entities $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ travel at constant (possibly distinct) speeds $v_q$ and $v_r$ along line-segment trajectories $τ_q$ and $τ_r$ inside $P$. We study the first-visibility time $ t^* = \min\bigl\{\,t \ge 0 \mid \overline{q(t)\,r(t)} \subseteq P\,\bigr\}, $ the earliest moment at which the segment joining $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ lies entirely within $P$. Prior work by Eades et al.~\cite{swat2020,eeades-phd} focused on the decision version of this question in a simple polygon. They gave a one-shot decision algorithm running in ${O}(n)$ time. For a stationary entity and a moving one, they gave a data structure with ${O}(n \log n)$ preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that answers decision queries in ${O}(\log n)$ time. For two moving entities, after ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ preprocessing time, they built a data structure of size ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ with ${O}(n^{3/4}\log^3 n)$ query time. Variants for polygonal domains with holes or when entities cross the boundary of $P$ lie beyond our scope. In this work, we go beyond decision to compute $t^*$ exactly under three models for a simple polygon $P$. When both trajectories are fixed in advance, we preprocess $P$ in ${O}(n)$ time and space and answer each query $(v_q, v_r)$ in ${O}(\log n)$ time. If one trajectory $τ_r$ is fixed while $τ_q$ is given as a query, we build a structure in ${O}(n \log n)$ time and space that computes $t^*$ in ${O}(\log^2 n)$ time per query. When neither trajectory is known in advance, we develop a data structure with ${O}(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ expected preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that achieves ${O}(n^{1/2}\,\text{polylog}(n))$ expected query time for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.

papers.title: Nearly-Tight Oracle Complexity of Packing and Covering Linear Programs
papers.abstract: We settle the deterministic oracle complexity of packing and covering linear programs, as measured by the number of oracle queries to the constraint matrix modeled by left and right matrix-vector products, up to a logarithmic factor. We do so by providing nearly-matching upper and lower bounds. Our algorithm breaks the $1/ε^2$ barrier of width-independent, $(1+ε)$-multiplicative error parallel solvers from prior work, improving the scaling with the error $ε>0$ to $1/ε,$ with total number of arithmetic operations scaling near-linearly with $1/ε$ and the number of nonzero entries of the constraint matrix.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Concurrent Stochastic Games: Exact Value and Approximation
papers.abstract: We consider two-player zero-sum concurrent stochastic games played over a finite state space for an infinite number of stages. In every stage, both players simultaneously and independently choose an action. Then, given the current state and chosen actions, the successor state is selected according to a stochastic transition function. We consider limit-average objectives, where Player 1 maximizes the long-run average of rewards assigned to every transition. The value from an initial state is the maximal expectation that Player 1 can ensure. We study the two basic computational problems: (a) the approximation problem of computing the values within an arbitrary additive error, and (b) the exact problem of deciding whether the value at a state is at least a given threshold. The previous results in the literature establish: (a) the approximation problem belongs to TFNP[NP], and (b) the exact problem belongs to PSPACE, via the theory of the reals, and is SQRT-SUM-hard. Our contributions are as follows. (a) Our main result shows that the approximation problem is in TFNP, and that the associated gap or promise problem is in NP $\cap$ coNP. (b) We also show that the exact problem is in $\exists\mathbb{R} \cap \text{co-}\exists\mathbb{R}$, i.e., it reduces to both the existential and the universal theory of the reals, and that it is PosSLP-hard.

papers.title: Coarse Price Discrimination
papers.abstract: We study the revenue cost of limiting a seller to $L$ posted prices when heterogeneous buyers with independent values compete for scarce inventory. Our large-market assumption requires that removing any buyer have little effect on optimal revenue. We first make buyers arbitrarily replaceable at each fixed stock and then let stock grow. In this limit, one price guarantees half of optimal mechanism revenue and two guarantee $e/(e+1)$, approximately $73.1\%$. For $L\ge3$, the corresponding guarantee is a $1-1/(2L-1)$ fraction. The guarantees accommodate arbitrary differences in demand across buyers and do not require a separate price for each customer group.

papers.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
papers.abstract: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.

papers.title: A Matrix Lee-Sidford Barrier and Faster Semidefinite Programming
papers.abstract: We construct a matrix analog of the Lee-Sidford barrier for semidefinite programming (SDP) with $m$ equality constraints and $n$-by-$n$ matrices. The barrier has self-concordance parameter $\widetilde{O}(m)$, so short-step interior-point methods require only $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$ iterations. We also show that our matrix Lee-Sidford barrier can be implemented efficiently by developing a randomized algorithm that solves SDPs with $m\leq n$ to accuracy $ε$ in $(n^{ω+o(1)}+n^2m^{3/2+o(1)})\operatorname{polylog}(1/ε)$ time, where $ω\leq 9/4$ is the matrix multiplication exponent, achieving the fastest known running time in this regime.

papers.title: Quantitative Convergence of Hit-and-Run Beyond Log-Concavity via Variational Hypocoercivity
papers.abstract: We study the convergence to equilibrium of Hit-and-Run, a popular generalisation of the Gibbs sampler. To this end, we establish a novel connection between Hit-and-Run and the theory of variational hypocoercivity, an approach to establish convergence of continuous-time Markov processes. To bridge the gap between the discrete-time Hit-and-Run chain and hypocoercivity, we introduce Hit-and-Langevin, a continuous-time Markov process that approximates Hit-and-Run in an appropriate sense. Using the second-order lift and flow Poincaré inequality formulation of variational hypocoercivity, we show convergence of Hit-and-Langevin and deduce a lower bound on the spectral gap of Hit-and-Run. Notably, our analysis seamlessly extends beyond the extensively studied setting of log-concave target distributions, marking the first substantial departure from this setting beyond quasi-log-concave and uniform distributions. More broadly, this work demonstrates that discrete, non-local dynamics, such as Hit-and-Run, can be made amenable to powerful analytical methods, such as variational hypocoercivity.

papers.title: Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals
papers.abstract: Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.

papers.title: First-Order Entropic Sampling of Words with Prescribed Letter Counts in Linear Time
papers.abstract: We sample, exactly and uniformly, a word of length n over the alphabet {0, . . . , r} in which the letter j occurs a prescribed positive number k j of times, from a source of fair random bits. Every exact sampler reads on average at least H = log 2 (___ n k0,...,kr )___ bits. We give a sampler that reads on average at most H fresh bits, whatever r and the counts, and that performs O(n) bit operations on average over every fixed alphabet, in a bit-RAM in which a memory access costs O(1) while arithmetic is charged bit by bit. Both bounds are optimal: the first one to first order, the second one up to a constant factor, since writing the output already costs $Θ$(n). The sampler writes the word as a Huffman tree of independent binary words, and samples each of them in one of two ways. Binary words with few ones are generated by random insertions; the rank of each inserted letter among its copies, which the Fisher-Yates shuffle generates for nothing, is uniform and independent of the word, and is given back to a recycling source of uniform integers, where it pays for the next insertions. Binary words with many ones are generated by MergeShuffle driven by blocks of $Θ$(log n) bits of entropy; a block is decoded by locating only its ones when the minority letter is rare, and otherwise, its number of ones being concentrated, by a precomputed table of the blocks of typical type, of size O( $\sqrt$ n log 4 n), the rare atypical blocks being decoded slowly.

papers.title: Location-Aware Matching Statistics
papers.abstract: Edit distance is the standard measure of string similarity, but its quadratic-time complexity is prohibitive for long strings. Popular linear-time alternatives, such as the $q$-gram distance, or the average common substring measure (ACS) that is based on matching statistics (MS), consider the substrings shared by the two input strings but not where they occur in each string. Yet in many real-world applications, e.g., when comparing document versions or co-recorded time series, a shared substring is really relevant only if its occurrences are close in position. We introduce Location-Aware Matching Statistics (LAMAS). Given strings $X$ and $Y$ and a displacement tolerance $d$, LAMAS reports, for every position $i$ of $Y$, the longest substring starting at $i$ that occurs in $X$ at a position $j$ with $|j-i|\le d$, together with the displacement $(j-i)$. MS is the special case of LAMAS with unbounded $d$. Our main result is an algorithm that solves LAMAS in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time and space for strings of length at most $n$ and any $d$; this is optimal and matches the complexity of MS. The algorithm reduces LAMAS to predecessor and successor queries over a sliding window of suffix ranks and answers them in linear total time via a window decomposition and interval union-find. Experiments on 20 real datasets and synthetic data show that LAMAS substantially improves over MS and $q$-gram distance in similarity-based classification, top-$K$ retrieval, and clustering. It is competitive with edit distance and a constrained dynamic time warping variant in classification and generally outperforms a state-of-the-art method for top-$K$ retrieval under edit distance. Finally, our implementation of the main algorithm for LAMAS scales linearly in $n$ and does not slow down as $d$ grows.

papers.title: Stay or Switch? Metric Distortion with Online Candidate Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study metric distortion in sequential elections with online candidate arrivals. In each round, a newly arriving challenger competes against the incumbent, and a voting rule must select one of the two based on voters' pairwise preferences. Our goal is to guarantee low metric distortion at every round, relative to the best candidate among all those that have arrived so far. For deterministic rules, we establish an asymptotically optimal bound of $Θ(\sqrt{t})$ at round $t$, achieved by a threshold rule favoring the incumbent. In contrast, randomization allows constant distortion. We show that persistent randomized dictatorship achieves optimal distortion of $5$ against adaptive adversaries, which observe previous winners, and $3$ against oblivious adversaries, which do not. Finally, we generalize the model along two dimensions, the available information and the action space, and establish distortion guarantees for each setting.

papers.title: A $(17/7-o(1))n$ Circuit Lower Bound for Binary-Encoded 3-SAT
papers.abstract: We strengthen the elementary $n-1$ circuit lower bound for a specified binary encoding of 3-SAT to $(17/7)n-O(n\log\log n/\log n)$ gates over the full two-input Boolean basis, with unrestricted depth and sharing. For each integer $w\ge5$, we encode 3-CNF formulas with exactly $m=2^w-1$ clauses over $m$ available variables using $n=3m(w+1)$ bits. The proof embeds Boolean tests in variable identifiers while retaining $n-o(n)$ free bits, and combines weighted gate elimination with a nonlinear-gate lower bound from the tests' full algebraic degree over $\mathbb F_2$. We provide Lean proofs of the finite inequality and the asymptotic bound for arbitrary acyclic binary circuits.

papers.title: How Much Randomness is Needed to Convert MA Protocols to AM Protocols?
papers.abstract: The Merlin-Arthur class of languages MA is included into Arthur-Merlin class AM, and into PP. For a standard transformation of a given MA protocol with Arthur's message (= random string) of length a and Merlin's message of length m to a PP machine, the latter needs O(ma)random bits. The same holds for simulating MA protocols by AM protocols: in the resulting AM protocol the length of Arthur's message (= random string) is O(ma). And the same holds for simulating heuristic MA protocols by heuristic AM protocols as well. In the paper [A.Knop, Circuit Lower Bounds for Average-Case MA, CSR 2015] it was conjectured that, in the transformation of heuristic MA protocols to heuristic AM protocols, O(ma) can be replaced by a polynomial of a only. A similar question can be asked for normal MA and AM protocols, and for the simulation of MA protocols by PP machines. In the present paper we show that, relative to an oracle, both latter questions answer in the negative and Knop's conjecture is false. Moreover, the same is true for simulation of MA protocols by AM protocols in which the error probability is not bounded away from 1/2, the so called PP.NP protocols. The latter protocols generalize both AM protocols and PP machines.

papers.title: Proper and Optimal Scoring Rules for Risk-Averse Agents
papers.abstract: Scoring rules are used to elicit probabilistic beliefs through payments that depend on reports and realised outcomes. We ask how these rules should be designed to induce truthful reporting and incentivise costly information acquisition when the agent is risk averse. For agents with entropic risk preferences in finite state spaces, we characterise proper scoring rules through an exponential transformation, derive optimal structures for information acquisition under bounded payments, and obtain explicit optimal coefficients in the binary case. The risk-neutral limit preserves properness and, in the binary case, optimality, while recovering the optimal betting structure for nonbinary states. For optimal design in the binary model, it suffices to focus on rules whose associated concave function is affine on each side of the prior. The optimal coefficients depend only on the prior and the risk-aversion parameter. The binary optimal rules we construct also admit an exact transformation from a particular risk-neutral optimal rule. In the nonbinary model, optimal design reduces to choosing the best prior bound in a transformed betting mechanism.

papers.title: $\mathrm{LogCFL} = \mathrm{UAux}\bigl(O(\log n),\mathrm{poly}(n)\bigr)$

notes: N. V. Vinodchandran has 4 papers across the five conferences

papers.title: Algorithms for Detecting Shape Defects in Concentrated Solar Power Plant Components
papers.abstract: Concentrated solar power (CSP) technology offers a dispatchable renewable energy solution, capable of bridging the gap between intermittent generation and grid demand through high-capacity thermal energy storage. However, the overall thermodynamic efficiency and cost-effectiveness of CSP plants depend crucially on the optical quality and precise geometric alignment of thousands of reflective surfaces spread across vast solar fields. Shape defect detection algorithms have become essential tools for automating mirror profilometry, tracking the flow spot and diagnosing alignment issues. This paper presents a novel framework for geometric shape detection techniques tailored to CSP applications. It introduces the notion of \emph{parabolicity}, which motivates a class of optimisation problems in this setting and suggests a possible direction for further work in computational geometry. Both exact and approximate algorithms are proposed, together with an experimental study on synthetic datasets generated via simulation.

papers.title: Optimizing Diameter of r-Gather under Connectivity Constraints from Convex to Connected
papers.abstract: The $r$-gather problem partitions the nodes of an edge-weighted graph into clusters of at least $r$ nodes each. The problem is NP-hard, and known approximation algorithms may return clusters whose induced subgraphs are disconnected. We therefore require each cluster to be connected, or even convex in the existential sense that some shortest path between any two of its members stays inside the cluster. We add a parameterized $α$-ratio-convex variant that interpolates between the two by bounding the induced stretch by a factor $α$. We measure the cost of a clustering by its diameter, the largest pairwise distance within a cluster, rather than by the radius as in the classical formulation. We show that the variants form a hierarchy, that they remain NP-hard in general, and that none of them admits a polynomial-time $(2-\varepsilon)$-approximation unless P=NP. Our main algorithmic result is a polynomial-time algorithm for convex $r$-gather on trees. This contrasts with connected $k$-diameter, which remains hard even on star-like connectivity graphs. On general weighted graphs, we give a $4$-approximation for connected $r$-gather. Extending the tree algorithm to tree decompositions, we obtain an exact algorithm for connected $r$-gather that is fixed-parameter tractable in the treewidth together with $d$ and $r$. Finally, we relate the $α$-ratio-convex variant to $t$-spanners, which yields further approximation guarantees.

papers.title: Tight Query Depth of Recursive Randomized Greedy MIS
papers.abstract: The randomized greedy maximal independent set (RGMIS) algorithm processes vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily constructs an MIS. Its recursive formulation decides whether a vertex belongs to this MIS by querying lower-ranked neighbors in increasing rank order, stopping when a neighbor in the MIS is found. We prove that, on every $n$-vertex graph, this recursive algorithm has $O(\log n)$ query depth with high probability, even without memoization. The bound holds simultaneously for all starting vertices and is asymptotically tight even on bipartite graphs. The proof combines a bound on the total expected number of query paths with an exposure argument: paths with many two-edge shortcuts are unlikely, while the remaining paths admit sufficiently many applications of a two-hop probability bound.

papers.title: How Do Deep Networks Encode and Selectively Use Information? Shared Encoding and Conditional Signed Readout in Vision and Language Models
papers.abstract: How can trained deep networks retain contextual information across internal representations while using it selectively in a decision? We study this question through controlled background-texture edits in vision classifiers and entity-binding edits in frozen language models. Across both modalities, factor perturbations preserve recognizable structure across pre-fixed, mutually disjoint blocks of hidden units: visual channel blocks match their complements more closely for the same image than for other images under the same texture edit, while language blocks transfer a relational direction fitted under one query role to rank relational states within held-out name pairs under the other role. We then decompose the local output change into signed channel and pathway contributions. In a convolutional classifier, net channel-level reinforcement ($R^{(512)}>1$) coexists on individual images with cancellation between positive- and negative-weight groups ($R^{(2)}<1$). Holding weights, the paired relation edit, and red/blue answer words fixed, switching prompt presentation reverses the mean finite selection effect in Qwen2.5. Two held-out tests validate this mechanism. Attenuating development-selected antagonistic units amplifies edit effects on unseen inputs; in a vision transformer, attenuating the same frozen units in one forward pass increases the mean magnitude of the background-edit effect on one class margin and reduces it on another, with the opposite pattern for a second group (four-cell paired interaction $+78.30\times 10^{-5}$ logit). Finally, combining conditional channel variance with fixed downstream readout weights predicts single-channel pruning recovery across ten cuts. These results show how shared encoding and conditional signed readout can coexist in vision and language models.

papers.title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
papers.abstract: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

papers.title: Toward Open Room-Scale Scanning with Consumer LiDAR via Depth-Inertial Odometry
papers.abstract: Room scanning with consumer LiDAR today depends on ARKit, whose tracking and map update are a black box: an application receives depth and poses but cannot inspect how they were produced, so an error in a scan cannot be traced to its cause. This paper examines whether an open alternative, one whose every stage can be inspected, is feasible on the device. Mobile-LIO is a depth-inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone's depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. papers.title: Principal Revelations of the Revelation Principle
papers.abstract: I prove a converse to the revelation principle, arguing that it is a principle of optimism: if it must hold for all environments (in fact, even just those with private values and independent types) the principal must assume her favorite equilibrium is played by the agents. When the principal knows only that the prior lies in some set, she must additionally assume it is her favorite one. With private values, independent types, and quasilinear payoffs, however, unrestricted transfers allow the principal to approximate any mechanism's equilibrium payoff via a direct mechanism whose unique equilibrium is truthful.
